newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - on edge over Iraqi exports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - on edge over Iraqi exports.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices are likely to remain on edge this week amid widening uncertainty over the timing of renewed Iraqi exports, traders and analysts said on Monday.

Iraq said last week it would not restart oil sales for the second phase of the U.N. "oil-for-food" accord until a new aid distribution plan was in place. U.N. officials said it was up to Baghdad to complete a plan, then submit to the United Nations for final approval.
Iraqi officials contend that aid distribution has not kept pace with oil sales, making it vital to have a distribution plan in place before new sales begin.

Despite the hiatus in oil sales, most U.N. sources believe oil exports will resume in early July once the distribution plan and a new pricing formula are set, but some traders and analysts are skeptical.

"The general concern is the timing of Iraqi exports," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York. "My gut feeling is that this oil could be a bit more delayed than than consensus has said so far. That could give some underpinning to the market if not outright strength."

July West Texas Intermediate was trading around $18.95-19.05 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) Monday afternoon, up around 20 cents from Friday's settlement but still within a predicted range.
Cash WTI/Cushing was running around eight to nine cents higher than the July screen price, factoring in the premium for exchange-for-physical (EFP) transactions.
The EFP premium has dropped from around 20 cents a barrel a week ago, reflecting diminishing concern about possible foreign crude deliveries against the July NYMEX contract that expires on June 20.
The Gulf Coast has witnessed fewer crude offerings from the North Sea and West Africa recently, reflecting the tight transatlantic arbitrage.

An East Coast cash trader echoed somewhat bullish perceptions in the short term. "We still have really high refinery utilization and strong gasoline demand. I just don't think there's much room on the downside."
Market-watchers were also looking to Tuesday's weekly inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) for general price direction.
Preliminary expecations are for slight builds in crude and gasoline.
"I think end-June crude stocks will be at or below last year. Stocks will stabilize because of high refinery runs," said Brown.
A meeting of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), scheduled for June 25, could give the market some background support.

"There could be some short-covering ahead of the OPEC meeting... but overall we're in a consolidation mode," said John Saucer, an analyst with Smith Barney in Houston. "The OPEC meeting will probably reinforce that consoldation."
